newsitem.title: FRANCE: European grains prices sag as demand withers.
newsitem.headline: European grains prices sag as demand withers.

text.p: Flagging demand and end-of-season farm selling drove most European grain prices down this week, while a strong British pound against other European Union currencies hit prices in the UK.

In France, new crop wheat dropped as farmers turned active sellers ahead of the new harvest. June delivery into Rouen was quoted at 815-820 francs per tonne, down 30 francs over last week. New crop prices also eased on favourable crop weather and a sluggish export scene.
Barley and maize were quiet but slipped in sympathy with wheat.
"It is an end-of-season market," one broker said.
Dealers attending an informal European grain trading session in Paris said the focus was now on the new harvest.
Overall crop conditions remained good as scattered showers and warm temperatures lingered over France this week.
But brokers said there might be "a few surprises" as April frost had raised fears of a deterioration in the quality of the barley crop.

On export markets, prospects for European grains remained bleak. On Thursday the European Union, anxious not to signal to the market that it was returning to the export scene, maintained taxes on wheat and flour exports despite lower prices.
A European grain official said the EU would not open free-market grain export tenders for 1997/98 "for the time being" out of caution ahead of the new crop.
German spot and new crop wheat prices eased in both delivered and export markets as generally well-covered buyers stopped putting in orders.
Expectations of an early wheat harvest, should the sunny weather persist, also helped drive down new crop prices.
Meanwhile feed wheat markets remained under pressure from British offers. Trading in barley and rye was very quiet.
Spot bread wheat prices on the Hamburg grain exchange were off five marks per tonne on the week to 277.50 marks and the feed wheat price was also off five at 275 marks.
Old and new crop barley indications were 262.50 marks and 240.00 marks, down 2.50 marks on the week.
Old and new crop rye was quoted at 260.00 and 255.00 marks respectively, also down 2.50 marks.
Trading in the British grain markets was dominated by currency, with strong sterling pressuring prices.
Sentiment that there was much more grain left on farms than earlier thought also hit prices on physical and futures markets.
"Currency has been the most important factor this week but there is a feeling that there is a lot more old crop grain left than people first thought," one broker said.
Farmers have been reluctantly selling new crop but with futures markets at contract lows they will only sell when they have to.
"There are a lot of shorts in the market, but farmers are hanging on until the harvest," said another broker.
This might, however, prove risky for farmers so close to the new harvest.
"We seem to be heading for a good crop this year and the rain forecast for the weekend makes the outlook even better," one broker said
Italian durum wheat prices fell over the past week as attention turned to the Spanish harvest, the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies said.
Maize prices fell by some 5,000 lire as poor quality maize discouraged even feed producers.

In Spain most grain prices, except milling wheat, eased ahead of the new harvest. But wheat prices could head higher as persistent rainfall this week halted the durum wheat harvest and raised concern over a deterioration in quality.
"I think the harvest is going to be higher than expected, but durum wheat's quality is going to be very bad," a Madrid-based broker said.
Another trader was more pessimistic, saying wheat production would be low, possibly creating a shortage of good quality grain and driving up prices.
"The price is going to be very, very high. Milling wheat of good quality in particular will have to imported," he said.
